content: Preterm birth (PTB) is a significant contributor to perinatal mortality and morbidity. Although the exact mechanisms underlying preterm labour (PTL) are not fully understood, there is evidence suggesting a link between maternal psychological stress and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Relaxation therapies, which include techniques such as meditation and massage, are often used to address stress. However, no systematic review has previously evaluated the impact of relaxation techniques on preventing PTL or PTB. This review specifically excludes hypnosis, as it is addressed in a separate Cochrane review. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of relaxation therapies in preventing or treating PTL and in preventing PTB. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register, CENTRAL, and CINAHL, up to December 14, 2011. Study authors were also contacted for additional information. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-randomized trials, and quasi-randomized trials that compared relaxation techniques to usual care, no treatment, or sham interventions. Two authors independently assessed the search results for eligible studies, and disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third author. Data were extracted using a standardized form and checked for accuracy. The risk of bias in the included studies was independently evaluated by two authors, with any differences resolved through discussion. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), while dichotomous outcomes were assessed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI. The review included 11 RCTs involving a total of 833 women. However, the findings were primarily based on single studies with small sample sizes. Many of the included studies lacked sufficient information on key methodological aspects, such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding. None of the studies assessed PTL or PTB as their primary outcome. The interventions, practices, and timing of the included studies varied significantly, and no clear, consistent hypotheses were identified. For women not in PTL, one study reported that relaxation therapy reduced maternal stress, as measured by the Anxiety Stress Scale, at 26 to 29 weeks of gestation (MD -7.04; 95% CI -13.91 to -0.17). Additional benefits of relaxation therapy, when combined with standard treatment, included increased infant birthweight (MD 285.00 g; 95% CI 76.94 to 493.06), higher rates of vaginal delivery (RR 1.52; 95% CI 1.13 to 2.04), lower rates of cesarean section (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.78), reduced maternal anxiety (MD -15.79; 95% CI -18.33 to -13.25), and reduced maternal stress (MD -13.08; 95% CI -15.29 to -10.87). For women in PTL, a single study found no significant difference in the rate of PTB between the intervention and control groups (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.59). The pooled analysis of two studies using a fixed-effect model showed no significant difference in infant birthweight (MD -5.68 g; 95% CI -174.09 to 162.74). In conclusion, the review provides some evidence that relaxation therapy during pregnancy can reduce maternal stress and anxiety. However, there is no evidence to suggest that relaxation therapy has an effect on preventing PTL or PTB. These findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited quality of the included studies.
